summary: Describes eight additional Diffie-Hellman groups for use in IETF protocols such as S/MIME, SSH, TLS and IKE, so implementers can share the same groups across protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive a shared secret using agreed public group parameters. RFC 5114 gathers eight groups with test data and explains how several IETF security protocols identify or use them.

subtitle: Parameters and test data for eight Diffie-Hellman groups used by IETF protocols.

tldr.problem: Implementers needed a shared RFC source for parameters and test data for additional Diffie-Hellman groups used across security protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5114 specifies three modular-exponentiation groups and five elliptic-curve groups, provides test data, and describes how the groups fit X.509, IKE, TLS, SSH, and S/MIME.
tldr.outcome: The document gives implementers group parameters and examples for checking implementations. It is Informational and does not require support for the groups.

today: RFC 5114 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Publish More Diffie-Hellman Groups
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman key agreement depends on public parameters that both parties use. RFC 5114 collects parameters and test data for eight groups so implementers can use a common set across protocols including IKE, TLS, SSH, and S/MIME.

Three groups had previously been specified for IKE, and five for TLS. The RFC puts all eight definitions, test data, and usage notes together to support interoperable implementations and FIPS validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Both parties need to use compatible public parameters to derive the same shared secret. This RFC gathers group definitions and test examples for implementers of several protocols.

sections.title: The Eight Group Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC defines three modular-exponentiation groups: a 1024-bit group with a 160-bit prime-order subgroup, and two 2048-bit groups with 224-bit and 256-bit subgroups. Each definition gives the prime, generator, and subgroup order.

It also defines five elliptic-curve groups of 192, 224, 256, 384, and 521 bits. Their definitions give the curve parameters, generator point, and group order. Appendix A supplies party key values and resulting shared-secret test data.
sections.plainLanguage: Three groups use modular exponentiation, and five use elliptic curves. Each group has fixed public values, and the RFC provides example inputs and outputs for testing.

sections.title: Using the Groups in Protocols
sections.content:
For X.509 certificates, the public keys and parameters use encodings defined in RFC 3279. IKE uses registered transform identifiers; this RFC lists identifiers for all eight groups. For elliptic-curve groups in IKE, it specifies using the payload format and shared-key derivation procedure in RFC 4753.

The document also explains how the groups relate to TLS, SSH, and S/MIME. The procedures differ by protocol: for example, S/MIME obtains the recipient's Diffie-Hellman parameters from a certificate, while SSH can transmit MODP parameters during key exchange under RFC 4419.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol has its own rules for carrying a group name, key, or parameter. RFC 5114 points implementers to those rules and lists the IKE group identifiers.

sections.title: Key Sizes and Assigned Identifiers
sections.content:
The strength of a Diffie-Hellman result depends on the group, the secret exponent size, and the randomness used. For MODP groups, the secret should match the subgroup size; for elliptic-curve groups, it must match the group order size. A larger secret does not add security, while a smaller one can reduce it.

The RFC provides approximate comparisons with symmetric and RSA key sizes. IANA updated the IKE and IKEv2 registries for five groups; the other three elliptic-curve groups were already listed in the IKE registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The private value must have the size appropriate for its group. A group name also needs a shared registry identifier so peers can select the same parameters.
